summary: Describes what the IETF community expects Internet Service Providers to do about security, including how they should handle incidents, protect their own infrastructure, and cooperate with customers. It is a Best Current Practice and invites discussion and improvements.

plainLanguage.summary: This document lists what the Internet community expects of an Internet service provider on security: published addresses to report abuse and attacks, an acceptable use policy, filtering of forged traffic at the edge of the network, and careful handling of the provider's own systems and mail servers.

subtitle: What the Internet community expects a service provider to do about security.

tldr.problem: Customers of an Internet service provider have no agreed baseline for what security the provider should offer, so the quality of protection depends on who they happen to sign up with.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets out expectations in four areas: how to reach the provider about security, what the acceptable use policy should say, how the provider should run its own network and systems, and how incidents are reported.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3013 is BCP 46 and is not obsoleted. It is explicitly not normative and says it does not dictate business practices.

today: RFC 3013 is a Best Current Practice document, BCP 46, and is neither obsoleted nor updated by any RFC listed for it. The document itself notes that it is a snapshot from 2000 and likely to become dated as other expectations arise.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
The purpose of this document is to express what the engineering community as represented by the IETF expects of Internet Service Providers (ISPs) with respect to security. It is addressed to ISPs, and by informing them of what the community hopes and expects of them, the community hopes to encourage ISPs to become proactive in making security a priority.

Under no circumstances is it the intention of the document to dictate business practices. It defines ISPs to include organisations in the business of providing Internet connectivity or other Internet services, including but not restricted to web hosting services, content providers and e-mail services, and does not include organisations providing those services for their own purposes.

The document is offered as a set of recommendations to ISPs regarding what security and attack management arrangements should be supported, and as advice to users regarding what they should expect from a high quality service provider. It is in no sense normative in its own right. In time it is likely to become dated, and other expectations may arise, but it represents a snapshot of the recommendations of a set of professionals in the field at a given point in the development of the Internet and its technology.
sections.plainLanguage: Read this as a checklist of what a reasonable provider is expected to do. It is guidance, not a standard that anyone audits against, and the document says so.

sections.title: Communication Channels for Security Matters
sections.content:
The community's most significant security-related expectations of ISPs relate to the availability of communication channels for dealing with security incidents.

ISPs should adhere to RFC 2142, which defines the mailbox SECURITY for network security issues, ABUSE for issues relating to inappropriate public behaviour and NOC for issues relating to network infrastructure. It also lists additional mailboxes defined for receiving queries and reports relating to specific services. They have a duty to make sure that their contact information, in Whois, in routing registries or in any other repository, is complete, accurate and reachable.

ISPs should have clear policies and procedures on sharing information about a security incident with their customers, with other ISPs, with Incident Response Teams, with law enforcement or with the press and general public, and should have processes in place to deal with incidents that traverse the boundaries between them and other ISPs. Such communication should be possible over a secure channel, noting that in some jurisdictions secure channels might not be permitted.

ISPs should be proactive in notifying customers of security vulnerabilities in the services they provide, and as new vulnerabilities in systems and software are discovered they should indicate whether their services are threatened by these risks. When an incident affects components of the ISP's infrastructure, the ISP should promptly report to customers who is coordinating the response, the vulnerability, how service was affected, what is being done to respond, whether customer data may have been compromised, what is being done to eliminate the vulnerability, and the expected schedule for response, assuming it can be predicted. Many ISPs already have procedures for notifying customers of outages, and it is reasonable to use those channels for security incidents, though the customer's normal point of contact will then receive the report rather than their security contact, so customers should route such notifications appropriately.

Whether or not an ISP has a Computer Security Incident Response Team (CSIRT), it should have a well-advertised way to receive and handle reported incidents from its customers, and should document its capability to respond. It should not be assumed that connectivity customers or an attacked site can automatically use the services of an ISP's CSIRT: ISP CSIRTs are frequently provided as an added-cost service, with the team defining as their constituency only those who subscribe to incident response services. Customers should therefore find out whether their ISP has a CSIRT and what its charter, policies and services are, so they can define their escalation chain before an incident occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider has to be reachable and has to say in advance what happens when something breaks. The addresses are fixed by convention: one for security, one for abuse, one for the network itself. And the provider should say up front whether it has an incident response team, because it may only serve paying subscribers of that service.

sections.title: Appropriate Use Policies
sections.content:
Every ISP should have an Appropriate Use Policy (AUP). Whenever an ISP contracts with a customer to provide connectivity, that contract should be governed by an AUP. The AUP should be reviewed each time the contract comes up for renewal, and the ISP should proactively notify customers as policies are updated.

An AUP should clearly identify what customers shall and shall not do on the various components of a system or network, including the type of traffic allowed on the networks. It should be as explicit as possible to avoid ambiguity or misunderstanding; an AUP might, for example, prohibit IP spoofing. In addition to communicating the AUP to customers, ISPs should publish it in a public place such as their web site, so that the community knows what the ISP considers appropriate and what action to expect in the event of inappropriate behaviour. An AUP should be clear in stating what sanctions will be enforced.

Many jurisdictions have Data Protection Legislation. Where such legislation applies, ISPs should consider the personal data they hold and, if necessary, register themselves as Data Controllers and be prepared to use the data only in accordance with the terms of the legislation. Given the global nature of the Internet, ISPs located where no such legislation exists should at least familiarise themselves with the idea of data protection by reading a typical Data Protection Act.
sections.plainLanguage: The contract should say what customers may and may not do, including what traffic is allowed, and the same text should be public so that everyone knows what the rules and the penalties are. Where privacy law applies, the provider has to think about what personal data it holds and register itself if the law says it must.

sections.title: Network Infrastructure: Registries and Routing
sections.content:
ISPs are responsible for managing the network infrastructure of the Internet in such a way that it is reasonably resistant to known security vulnerabilities, and not easily hijacked by attackers for use in subsequent attacks.

ISPs are commonly responsible for maintaining the data stored in global repositories such as the Internet Routing Registry and the APNIC, ARIN and RIPE databases. Updates to this data should only be possible using strong authentication. ISPs should also publicly register the address space that they assign to their customers, so that there is more specific contact information for the delegated space.

An ISP's ability to route traffic to the correct destination may depend on routing policy as configured in routing registries. If so, and if the registry supports it, the ISP should ensure that the registry information it maintains can only be updated using strong authentication, and that the authority to make updates is appropriately restricted. Due care should also be taken in determining in whose routing announcements to place greater trust when a choice of routes is available; in the past, bogus announcements have resulted in traffic being black holed, or worse, hijacked. BGP authentication should be used with routing peers.
sections.plainLanguage: The records that say who owns which addresses and which routes must only be changeable by the right people, with strong authentication. Otherwise an attacker changes a record, routes traffic to themselves, and the network either breaks or is quietly taken over.

sections.title: Filtering Traffic at the Customer Edge
sections.content:
Attackers frequently cover their tracks by using forged source addresses. To divert attention from their own site, the source address they choose will generally be from an innocent remote site, or from addresses allocated for private Internets. Forged source addresses are also frequently used in spoof-based attacks in order to exploit a trust relationship between hosts.

Ingress filtering has the direction from the edge site, the customer, to the Internet. At the boundary router with each of their customers, ISPs should proactively filter all traffic coming from the customer that has a source address of something other than the addresses that have been assigned to that customer. There are rare circumstances where ingress filtering is not currently possible, for example on large aggregation routers that cannot take the additional load of applying packet filters, and such filtering can cause difficulty for mobile users. Where ingress filtering at the interface between the customer and the ISP is not possible, the customer should be encouraged to implement ingress filtering within their own networks, and in general filtering should be done as close to the actual hosts as possible.

Egress filtering has the direction from the Internet to the edge site. There are many applications in widespread use that grant trust to other hosts based only on the IP address, such as the Berkeley r commands, and these are susceptible to IP spoofing. There are also vulnerabilities that depend on the misuse of supposedly local addresses, such as the land attack. At the boundary router with each of their customers, ISPs should therefore filter all traffic going to the customer that has a source address of any of the addresses that have been assigned to that customer.

Excessive routing updates can be leveraged by an attacker as a base load on which to build a denial of service attack, and at the very least they result in performance degradation. ISPs should filter the routing announcements they hear, for example to ignore routes to addresses allocated for private Internets, to avoid bogus routes and to implement BGP Route Flap Dampening and aggregation policy. They should implement techniques that reduce the risk of putting excessive load on routing in other parts of the network, including nailed up routes, aggressive aggregation and route dampening, all of which lower the impact on others when internal routing changes in a way that is not relevant to them.

The IP protocol allows for directed broadcast, the sending of a packet across the network to be broadcast onto a specific subnet. Very few practical uses for this feature exist, but several different security attacks, primarily denial of service attacks making use of the packet multiplication effect of the broadcast, use it. Therefore, routers connected to a broadcast medium must not be configured to allow directed broadcasts onto that medium.
sections.plainLanguage: At the edge of each customer's connection, the provider should drop packets that claim to come from an address the customer does not own, and packets arriving for the customer that claim to come from the customer's own address space. That stops a customer from forging traffic in either direction, which is what most spoofing attacks and some denial of service tricks rely on.

sections.title: Systems Infrastructure
sections.content:
The way an ISP manages its systems is crucial to the security and reliability of the network. A breach of those systems may minimally lead to degraded performance or functionality, but could lead to loss of data or the risk of traffic being eavesdropped, leading to man-in-the-middle attacks. It is widely accepted that it is easier to build secure systems if different services, such as mail, news and web hosting, are kept on separate systems.

All systems that perform critical ISP functions, such as mail, news and web hosting, should be restricted so that access is only available to the administrators of those services. That access should be granted only following strong authentication, and should take place over an encrypted link. Only the ports on which those services listen should be reachable from outside the ISP's systems networks. ISPs should stay up to date with more secure methods of providing services as they become available. Systems should not be attached to transit network segments.

ISPs should take active steps to prevent their mail infrastructure from being used by spammers to inject unsolicited bulk e-mail while hiding the sender's identity, and should strongly encourage their customers to take the necessary steps to prevent this activity on their own systems.

Message submissions should be authenticated using the AUTH SMTP service extension. SMTP AUTH is preferred over IP address-based submission restrictions because it gives customers the flexibility of being able to submit mail even when not connected through the ISP's network, is more resistant to spoofing, and can be upgraded to newer authentication mechanisms as they become available. To facilitate the enforcement of security policy, it is strongly recommended that messages be submitted using the MAIL SUBMIT port (587) rather than through the SMTP port (25), so that the SMTP port can be restricted to local delivery only. The reason is to differentiate between inbound local delivery and relay, allowing customers to send email via the ISP's SMTP service to arbitrary receivers on the Internet; non-authenticated SMTP should only be allowed for local delivery. These measures not only protect the ISP from serving as an injection point via third-party relay, but also help in tracking accountability for message submission.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider's own machines are the softest target, so each service runs on its own machine, administration needs strong authentication over an encrypted link, and only the service ports are reachable from outside. Mail servers must not relay mail for strangers, and customers should log in to submit mail, on port 587 rather than port 25, so that port 25 can be limited to local delivery.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations section of this document consists of one sentence: the entire document discusses security issues. Everything in it, from the contact mailboxes through the acceptable use policy to ingress and egress filtering and the mail configuration, is a security measure, and the document asks that the providers who read it treat the recommendations as such.
sections.plainLanguage: There is nothing extra to add: every part of this document is about security, which is why the section is one line long.
